findings.summary: _make_hash drops the eq_key transformation for hashed attributes, so attributes declared with eq_key/eq=callable are now hashed by raw value, not by their key function. This changes hash values and can break the hash/eq contract.
findings.evidence: The removed branch in _make_hash (diff lines 1716-1724) previously did `if a.eq_key: globs[cmp_name] = a.eq_key; append '_<name>_key(self.<name>),'`. The new loop always emits `self.<name>,`. _make_eq (src/attr/_make.py:1786-1791, unchanged) still wraps values with the eq_key function. So __eq__ compares key(self.x) while __hash__ hashes self.x. Two objects that compare equal under the key can have different hashes. The removed `globs` dict is also gone, so the generated __hash__ can no longer reference key functions at all. Attribute.eq_key is documented as a field used for equality, and hash generation should stay consistent with it.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the eq_key branch in append_hash_computation_lines and keep `globs` passed to _make_method. The simplification should only drop the unused `globs=None` plumbing if it is truly unused, not remove key handling. Add a test with attr.ib(eq=callable, hash=True) that checks hash agrees with key-based equality.

findings.summary: The `_frozen_setattrs` rewrite changes runtime behavior on CPython: the `BaseException` exemption for `__cause__`/`__context__`/`__traceback__` is now compiled only into the PyPy branch, so on CPython every assignment on a frozen exception class raises FrozenInstanceError.
findings.evidence: Old code (diff '-' side) allowed `__cause__`, `__context__`, `__traceback__` on any BaseException for all interpreters. New code at src/attr/_make.py:587-599 has the exemption only under `if PYPY:`, and the `else:` branch (line 602-607) raises FrozenInstanceError unconditionally. The CPython path therefore rejects `exc.__cause__ = ...` and `exc.__traceback__ = ...` on frozen exception classes, which previously worked. Also, the PyPy branch silently dropped `__traceback__` from the allowed names, so PyPy behavior changes too. No test in tests/ covers `__traceback__` on frozen exceptions (search returned no matches), so the regression would not be caught; the only related test (tests/test_next_gen.py:295-313) covers `raise ... from None` only.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the original single `_frozen_setattrs` with all three names allowed for every interpreter. If a PyPy-specific split is genuinely needed, keep the same allowed set in both branches and add a test assigning `__cause__`/`__context__`/`__traceback__` on a frozen exception.

findings.summary: Removing the read1 override and the _CHUNK_SIZE=1 setting changes echo behavior for echo_stdin. Reads through read1 bypass echoing, and the buffered TextIOWrapper echoes a whole chunk on first read.
findings.evidence: The removed comment at the old lines near input._CHUNK_SIZE = 1 said: 'Force unbuffered reads, otherwise the underlying EchoingStdin stream will echo a big chunk of input on the first read.' The diff removes that setting, so the wrapper reads with the default chunk size. EchoingStdin also no longer defines read1, so the __getattr__ fallback (line 19-20) sends any read1 call straight to the underlying stream without echoing. This loses the per-read echo guarantee that the existing echo_stdin tests (tests/test_testing.py:29-32, 52-55) rely on.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep input._CHUNK_SIZE = 1 when echo_stdin is set, and keep an EchoingStdin.read1 that echoes. Verify with the echo_stdin tests, which could not run here because of an environment error.

findings.summary: With echo_stdin=True, visible_input now echoes the input twice: EchoingStdin already writes the consumed line to output, and visible_input writes it again.
findings.evidence: src/click/testing.py:205-206 wraps stdin in EchoingStdin when echo_stdin is set. visible_input (line 230) calls input.readline(), which goes through EchoingStdin._echo and writes the line to bytes_output. Line 231 then unconditionally writes f"{val}\n" to sys.stdout. The removed guard was `if not self.echo_stdin:`, which existed precisely to avoid this double write.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the guard: only write val+newline in visible_input when not self.echo_stdin.

That pause was removed along with EchoingStdin.paused and _echo's check, so line 238 readline() goes through EchoingStdin._echo and writes the hidden value to bytes_output. The same applies to _getchar(echo=False) at lines 240-245, which now echoes characters that should be hidden.
finding.suggested_fix: Keep the paused mechanism for echo_stdin, or otherwise suppress echoing for hidden input and non-echo getchar. Add a test with hide_input=True and echo_stdin=True asserting the secret is absent from output.

findings.summary: Swapping the assignment order changes which context supplies `args`. The leftover args are now read from the parent `ctx` instead of the newly created `sub_ctx`, so completion after a subcommand is resolved with the wrong args.
findings.evidence: In the original code, `ctx = sub_ctx` ran before `args = ctx._protected_args + ctx.args`, so args came from the sub context. The diff moves `args = ctx._protected_args + ctx.args` above `ctx = sub_ctx` (src/click/shell_completion.py:570-571). At that point `ctx` is still the parent group context, so args are taken from the parent. The same reordering happens in the chained-group branch (lines 589-590): `args = sub_ctx.args` now reads the previous sub_ctx instead of sub_sub_ctx. This is not a no-op refactor. The reordering changes values. The existing tests pass (run_tests tests/test_shell_completion.py: 41 passed), so the suite does not cover this path.
findings.suggested_fix: Revert the two reorderings: assign `ctx = sub_ctx` (and `sub_ctx = sub_sub_ctx`) before reading `args` from them, as in the original code. Add a test for completion of a nested subcommand's arguments so this regression is caught.

findings.summary: TextChunker.decode with chunk_size=None now returns [""] for empty input instead of [], so Response.iter_text() can yield empty strings that it did not yield before.
findings.evidence: httpx/_decoders.py:214-215 now reads `if self._chunk_size is None: return [content]`. Previously it returned `[content] if content else []`. In httpx/_models.py:854-856 (iter_text), `decoder.flush()` returns "" for an empty body and it is passed straight to `chunker.decode(text_content)`, which now yields "" to the caller. The same applies whenever a byte chunk decodes to empty text (e.g. a partial multibyte or compressed chunk). The existing tests in tests/models/test_responses.py (test_iter_text, test_aiter_text) and tests/test_decoders.py pass (140 passed), but none assert that an empty body produces zero text chunks, so the regression is not caught. This is a public API change for iter_text() and aiter_text(), and the task only asked for a simplification.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the `if content` guard in TextChunker.decode for the chunk_size=None path, i.e. `return [content] if content else []`. Only remove the `# pragma: no cover` markers if the branch is actually covered by tests. If the simplification is wanted, add a test asserting that iter_text on an empty body yields nothing and confirm the behavior is unchanged first.

findings.summary: FileField.get_length now returns the character count, not the byte count, for str file contents containing non-ASCII characters.
findings.evidence: httpx/_multipart.py:90-91 now does `return len(headers) + len(self.file)` for `str` file values. The removed line used `to_bytes(self.file)`, which encodes str to UTF-8 (httpx/_utils.py:325-326), so the old length was the byte length. `len()` on a str counts code points, so e.g. 'é' gives 1 here but 2 bytes on the wire. The Content-Length computed from get_length will then be wrong for such files, and the body rendered via render_data/encode will not match it. `FileContent` includes str, so this path is reachable.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore byte-length semantics, e.g. `return len(headers) + len(to_bytes(self.file))`, or `len(self.file.encode('utf-8'))` for str and `len(self.file)` for bytes. Add a test with a non-ASCII str file to check Content-Length.

findings.summary: Removing the `if buf:` guard makes split_before yield a spurious empty list for empty input (and for any input where the final buffer is empty), changing observable output.
findings.evidence: more_itertools/more.py:1227-1238: `buf = []`, then `for item in it:` never runs for an empty iterable, so the unconditional `yield buf` at line 1238 emits `[]`. Before the change the function yielded nothing for empty input. The sibling branch at line 1223-1224 (`maxsplit == 0`) yields `list(iterable)` and returns, so the empty-input behavior is now `[]` for maxsplit=-1 but `[[]]`-style results elsewhere are inconsistent. The existing tests (tests/test_more.py:1223-1273) cover only non-empty inputs, which is why the suite still passes (463 passed per Layer 1). No test covers `list(split_before([], pred))`.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the guard: `if buf: yield buf`. A behavior-preserving simplification is not available here; the guard is required for empty input and for the case where the separator is the last item only if buf is non-empty. If the simplification is intended, add a test asserting the new empty-input behavior and document it in docs/versions.rst.

findings.summary: Repeating before materializing breaks one-shot iterator inputs when repeat > 1. In gray_product, `iterables * repeat` repeats references to the same iterator object, so the first copy is consumed by `tuple(...)` and later copies become empty, causing a spurious ValueError (or wrong output) where ...
findings.evidence: Old code (more.py:4900 before the diff) did `tuple(map(tuple, iterables)) * repeat`, materializing each input once and then repeating the immutable tuples. New code does `tuple(map(tuple, iterables * repeat))`. For `gray_product(g, repeat=2)` with a generator g, `iterables * 2` is `(g, g)`; `tuple(g)` consumes g, so the second `tuple(g)` is `()` and line 4903 raises "each iterable must have two or more items". The same applies to partial_product at line 4942: `map(iter, (g, g))` yields the same iterator twice, so the elements are shared and the product is wrong instead of equal to partial_product(g_list, g_list, ...). The existing tests (tests/test_more.py:6007-6013) only use strings and lists, so they do not catch this. No test uses a generator with repeat.
findings.suggested_fix: Materialize inputs once before repeating, e.g. `all_iterables = tuple(map(tuple, iterables)) * repeat` as before in gray_product, and in partial_product `iterators = tuple(map(iter, tuple(map(tuple, iterables)) * repeat))`, or `iterables = tuple(map(tuple, iterables)); iterators = tuple(map(iter, iterables * repeat))`. Add a test with generator inputs and repeat>1.
